### From Schrodinger's cat to Heisenberg's uncertainty principle, this book untangles the weirdness of the quantum world. 'A master of making the complex simple' Independent 'Al-Khalili is the ideal guide through [the] mysteries of modern science' New Scientist 'Superb' Guardian
Quantum mechanics underpins modern science and provide us with a blueprint for reality itself. And yet it has been said that if you're not shocked by it, you don't understand it. But is quantum physics really so unknowable? Is reality really so strange? And just how can cats be half-alive and half-dead at the same time?
Our journey into the quantum begins with nature's own conjuring trick, in which we discover that atoms - contrary to the rules of everyday experience - can exist in two locations at once. url_citation.title: Jim Al-Khalili interview: why quantum is the spookiest science | Institute of Physics
url_citation.content:
‘Zombie cat’

At the centre of quantum strangeness lies superposition – the idea that something can exist in multiple states at once. In 1935, physicist Erwin Schrödinger illustrated it with his now-famous thought experiment: a cat, sealed in a box, that is suspended between life and death until observed.
In Quantum: A Guide for the Perplexed, Al-Khalili lays out the paradox: the cat’s fate is tied to a single radioactive atom, and until the box is opened, the entire system exists in superposition – both outcomes at once. “It’s a thought experiment that illustrates something real: quantum systems don’t behave like anything in our everyday world. They don’t pick a side until we look.”
When Al-Khalili talks about Schrödinger’s cat, there’s an amused softness to his voice – as if he knows he’s about to walk us to the edge of something deeply unsettling. “People love to call it the ‘zombie cat’,” he says, half-smiling. “And to be honest, that’s not a bad way of putting it.

...

“But nature may have been using quantum tricks billions of years before we even knew they existed.”
One of the most striking examples is the so-called quantum robin.

...

“We think entangled electrons in a light-sensitive molecule act like a kind of biological compass,” Al-Khalili explains. “That’s extraordinary – it means a living creature is, in effect, performing a quantum measurement just to find its way home.”
Photosynthesis, too, may lean on quantum effects.
